speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would invite Member to seek clarifications today, if need be.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And if the question has been addressed, it may not be necessary for her to proceed with the question for future Sitting.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I will first provide some background on the different methods of funding for healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For various reasons – asymmetry of information between doctors and patients, the moral hazard of insurance, the anxiety of patients and their loved ones – healthcare is highly susceptible to funding wastage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Better funding methods can reduce such wastage, without affecting service quality.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, funding by workload, such as the number of procedures, surgeries, scans, hospital bed days, does not in itself incentivise hospitals to be more targeted and efficient in delivering healthcare services, because all activities will be funded anyway.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Bundled payments, which are commonly practised around the world, help to remove what are known as disease-level operational inefficiencies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This means that hospitals get funded per care episode, rather than based on a detailed breakdown of workload.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We had implemented the bundled payments pilots, which allowed institutions to generate cost savings, for instance, by facilitating earlier transitions from acute hospitals to community hospitals, where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As hospitals attend to patients with varying degrees of disease severity, some requiring more interventions than others, so, bundled payment rates are set at an average to cover the total cost of all care episodes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This provides an incentive for the hospital to be more efficient.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Another model is pay-for-performance which provides financial incentives for clusters to perform well in key priority areas.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our pilot projects delivered positive results, leading to better health outcomes without compromising care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, these mechanisms, such as bundled payments by care episode, do not in themselves incentivise the reduction of what is known as population level wastage, that is, some patients should not become sick in the first place where preventive steps could have been taken in homes or communities to keep the residents healthy, before they become patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Capitation funding aims to incentivise healthcare providers to place a greater emphasis on preventive care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Under this funding model, healthcare providers are assigned a population base and are paid a pre-determined amount per resident under their charge.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They will thus be encouraged to incur a lower cost by intervening upstream and early to keep the patient healthy, knowing that it will require them to spend more to treat or cure patients in hospitals after they fall sick.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This method of funding is commonly practised around the world as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Different methods of funding for healthcare, be it bundled payments or capitation, if designed and implemented well, will not negatively affect the quality of service at hospitals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If wastage and unnecessary procedures can be removed, it will improve the effectiveness of our healthcare workers as well as their well-being, it will reduce the financing burden of healthcare and can improve the level of service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each cluster will be paid funding rates based on the age bands of their residents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The rates are designed so that there is no reduction – and in fact a slight increase, to the cluster budgets in previous years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As our population gets older, more residents will require higher capitation rates and the clusters will correspondingly receive higher budgets.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We maintain a flexible system where residents can continue to choose which hospitals they would like to go to and need not go to only the hospitals from the cluster that they are assigned to.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Transfer payments between clusters will be made to take this into account.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With capitation funding, the Ministry of Health (MOH) sets priority areas and key indicators for the immediate, medium and long term, while the public healthcare clusters have the mandate and operational flexibility to decide the resource allocation across their institutions and services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These key indicators were outlined in the White Paper on Healthier SG.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Healthcare clusters will take into account various factors when deciding how to allocate their funds.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These factors may include the cost of operations incurred by various healthcare institutions under their charge, the mix of residents that they serve and the performance management system under that cluster.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It does not mean that cluster have to pass through the funding mechanism in the form of capitation funding to their individual health institutions, which may not be practical.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, with capitation at the cluster level, there is a strong incentive for the clusters to invest more in primary and preventive care, and to work with all community partners, to help their residents stay healthy or delay disease progression.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We should expect many more initiatives in the preventive care space in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have two supplementary questions to each of the PQs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, under the capitation model, will there be a system in place to review the exceptional cases where patients outlive their prognosis or if their illness do not follow through the usual trajectory and ensure that care is not denied for these cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, given the rapid advancement in technology, especially in medical devices and pharmacology, how often are the care protocols reviewed, such that the capitation model and formulas are kept relevant with the most cost-effective treatments available?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, under the capitation model, will physicians be less incentivised to think out of the box to treat patients with complex clinical conditions as it may require costlier treatments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And lastly, while it is part of the plan for Healthier SG to stick with one general practitioner (GP), will capitation restrict patient choices for tertiary care as they will now be covered under regional area and served by a particular hospital?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first was whether there would be an issue around exceptional cases that do not follow the usual trajectory for diseases and the short answer is that, this is not a problem.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And it does not change the way in which the individual care decisions are made.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Capitation is a funding mechanism at a large population level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It does not remove the various other governance mechanisms that are in place across our healthcare system from the professional boards, the licensing boards, the interface with research and academia and the clinical review processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All of these will continue to review care protocols to make sure the care that is delivered is entirely appropriate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yip also asked if there is less incentive to innovate and think out the box?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That the personal level or the individual level of the clinicians will of course continue to be driven by their professional desire to provide the best possible care, whether it is following a standard protocol well demonstrated or whether it is looking for innovative ways to deal with unusual and exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the system level, the idea is to put in place mechanisms that drive innovation and thinking to be able to derive efficiencies, but more importantly, better care through the resources that we have.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I just have two supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My first question is that, if capitation is a method of encouraging less wastage and more preventive and primary care, how is MOH monitoring that clusters even with operational flexibility given, is actually channelling more of their resources towards primary and preventive care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second question is, towards the health outcomes that the clusters are asked to work towards for the funding, can the Senior Minister of State give an example of how a cluster will be incentivised to shift the capitation funding towards where we are directionally moving, preventive and primary care, rather than what they are doing today, it could be just for volume.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the first, how will we know that they are indeed channelling resources to primary and preventive care, well, we work very closely with the clusters on a day-to-day basis, with the clinicians at all levels of our healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The healthcare services have to interface with MOH on licensing decisions, on regulatory decisions, on the provision of resources.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, we will indeed have very close feel of where manpower resources and effort across our healthcare system is being asserted and will then know whether or not these measures around funding and around governance are resulting in the operational changes and the service delivery changes that we are hoping for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And we will pay very close attention to this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am a little hesitant because the whole idea is indeed to incentivise the clinicians and the service delivery teams to be able to think through what works best for their residents and their clinical service teams and their operational model.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But a hypothetical example, let us say something like diabetes, if you wanted to institute some particular care around diabetic eye disease, for example, you may choose to do this essentially and through the Eye Centre, through the ophthalmologists; or you may choose to do this on a screening basis and perhaps increase the capability at the level of the polyclinics, in the GPs to be able to detect this early; or you could potentially even go into the community and explain how having good care around your diabetes can prevent eye disease from happening in the first place.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And clearly, what we hope would be that the clusters and the professionals would do more of the third and prioritise the third and we should see that type of approach happening.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is an example, I do not know if that is the best example, but I think the examples and the specific clinical initiatives need to come from the professionals and the care teams that are involved.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have one question for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the capitation payment include all charges that the GP will charge the patient, meaning the capitation payment will include both the consultation and the drug cost of each visit by the patient?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the question that he is asking, in a way does not apply to the issue of capitation funding.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: A very brief supplementary question, please, Mr Leong, and then we will move on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State then, I think the issue that Singaporeans are most interested in is – I do not know whether MOH already got conclusion on that – is how will the outpatient patients be charged under the new Healthier SG scheme.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Capitation is about how we assign our budget to the clusters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What he is asking about is how will patients be charged when they go and see their GP, whether you have a Healthier SG programme or whether you are going for a fee for service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is not what we are talking about when we mean capitation funding, which is a way of deciding how to assign the MOH budget to the clusters, to hospitals and to different services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I appreciate that he may indeed be reflecting the concern of resident citizens about how they are charged, I believe those issues have been discussed at some length and are available in a fairly transparent and documented way at a number of sites, but perhaps today is not the place or the time to debate them.
